title: Starting the site

turns.text:
I want to start a personal blog, and also have my personal webpage. in my blog I want to post about topics I am interested in - AI, music, games, what I learned, and also something like a dev diary for this village project - I think it's so interesting on so many different levels, I just want to share my progress, updates, why I think it's important, and also by writing I'd improve my writing skills and also get a better understanding of how it actually works. I don't want to write my posts with AI explicitly, but I will need my AI's input on things, or prepare a paragraph which I'd quote explicitly as something by claude,  or get me some assets for a publication like before/after shots, etc. I'm going to have some code blocks potentially to demonstrate ideas. If there'd be a way to render certain 3d models or scenes inline using the game engine within the blog post that'd be totally amazing, too. Like, if i'm talking about an improvement in algorithm of generating a 3d model from an image - i'd like to embed before after models you could rotate, for example.

I need an extremely easy and convenient way to post and edit what I want. 

What do you think?

turns.text:
I'd build it as one small site that you own: a home page plus a blog. Posts would be plain text files in a Git repo, and a push publishes them. Hosted platforms like Ghost or Substack have nicer editors, but they can't host an interactive 3D viewer, and that's the feature that would make your blog stand out.

## Writing and editing
- **Each post is one folder.** It holds `index.mdx` (Markdown with a few extra tags) and its images, clips and models. You drag a screenshot into the folder and reference it by name.
- **Write wherever you like.** Obsidian, iA Writer, VS Code or the GitHub app on your phone all work, because a post is just a text file.
- **One command does the routine steps.** `new "title"` creates the folder and header. `preview` opens the site locally. `publish` pushes it, and the site rebuilds in about a minute. A post marked `draft: true` stays hidden until you remove the flag.
- **Fixing a typo later** means editing the file and publishing again.

I'd use Astro with MDX for this. It's a standard way to build a static blog, and it lets interactive parts load only where a post uses them. Pages stay fast and hosting is free. If you want a visual editor on top, Git-based options exist (Keystatic is one), but I haven't checked their current state.

## What goes in a post
- **Code blocks:** normal Markdown fences, highlighted when the site builds, with line highlighting and diffs available.
- **Claude's input:** a visible quote block like `<Claude model="Opus 5.5">…</Claude>`, styled so readers can see it isn't your text, and optionally showing the question you asked. I won't write your prose. I'll answer questions, give feedback when you ask, and write quotes that are clearly labelled as mine.
- **Assets:** I'll put before/after screenshots, short clips and comparison sliders straight into the post's folder. Anything from Village uses made-up names and test data. [redacted]

## 3D you can rotate
There are two levels of this:
1. **Possible now:** a `<Compare before="old.glb" after="new.glb" />` tag that shows two models side by side, each draggable to rotate, with the cameras linked. It would use Google's `model-viewer`, an open-source component, so there's little custom code. The catch is that the engine stores made things as cells and programs, not meshes, so I'd need to add a "save as .glb" export to the engine. That's worth having in Village anyway.
2. **Needs a short experiment:** the real engine running inside a post. Right now the engine's page depends on its local server: `link.ts`, `ask.ts` and `making.ts` all call it. A post would need a stripped-down viewer that loads a saved scene with no server and no making or talking. I don't know yet how hard that is, so I'd run a time-boxed test. It would also publish part of the engine's code.

## The personal page
The home page would be a short intro, a "now" section, your projects (Village first), your latest posts and your links. It's the same site, so there's nothing extra to maintain. Tags (AI, music, games, Village diary) give each topic its own feed.

## Before it goes live
It should be its own repo, separate from Village. Making it public needs your OK, and so does a domain if you want one. I have no standing permission to deploy anything publicly.

**One question:** where do you most like to write: Obsidian, iA Writer, a plain editor, or your phone? That decides which editing setup I build first.

After that I can make a first version for you to try: the home page and one sample post with a code block, a Claude quote and a rotatable before/after pair. You'd judge it by actually publishing something.

Twelve personal sites checked, plus three game-dev/graphics sites. Header, HTML and URL probes were all run live with curl on 2026-11-16. Items marked (inf) are inferred, not seen.

| Site | Generator | Host | Posts stored as | llms.txt | RSS | .md version | Accept: text/markdown | Notable |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| karpathy.ai | hand-written HTML + CSS | Fastly (x-served-by) | static page, no posts | 200 but it returns the HTML homepage (soft 404) | none | no | no | Says "I have three blogs": github.io (oldest), Medium, Bear |
| karpathy.bearblog.dev | Bear Blog | Cloudflare in front of Heroku | Bear's hosted DB | 301 | atom `/feed/` and rss `?type=rss` | no | no | Minimal CSS and zero JS, no embeds |
| simonwillison.net | Django (public repo simonw/simonwillisonblog) | Cloudflare in front of Heroku | Postgres, Datasette-powered | 404 | atom `/atom/everything/` | no | no | Blogmarks and notes; Datasette backs the search |
| leerob.com | Next.js | Vercel | (inf) MDX in git; his repo wasn't found under that name | 404 | none found at common paths | no | no | RSC `Vary` headers |
| overreacted.io | Next.js app router (public repo gaearon/overreacted.io, TypeScript) | Cloudflare (`public/_headers` and `_redirects` in repo, so Pages-style, inf) | MDX/MD in git | 200, real, lists `.../index.md` links | rss and atom | yes, `/<post>/index.md` returns text/markdown | no (returns html) | Posts are authored in the repo; he also writes about AT Protocol |
| joshwcomeau.com | Next.js | Vercel | (inf) MDX in git, closed source | 307 (redirect, not a file) | `/rss.xml` | no | no | Known for heavy interactive widgets (inf from his writing, not measured here) |

| swyx.io | SvelteKit | Cloudflare | (inf) git or CMS | 200, real, with description | `/rss.xml` | no | no | llms.txt present |

| danluu.com | (inf) Jekyll on GitHub Pages (x-github-request-id) | GitHub Pages behind Cloudflare | Markdown in git (inf) | 404 | `/atom.xml` | no | no | Near-zero CSS and JS |
| mitchellh.com | Next.js | Vercel | (inf) MDX in git | 404 | `/feed.xml` | no | no | |
| brandur.org | custom Go static generator (public repo brandur/sorg) | S3 + CloudFront | Markdown in git, compiled to static files | 404 | two atom feeds (articles, atoms) | no | no | Static output uploaded to S3 |
| iquilezles.org | hand-built / static (inf) | Apache | static HTML | not tested | not tested | not tested | no | Graphics articles with live WebGL demos (inf) |

| fabiensanglard.net | custom static, Apache | Apache | static HTML | not tested | not tested | not tested | no | Game-engine teardowns |

I also looked at noelberry.ca (nginx on Ubuntu, so self-hosted), lexaloffle.com (Cloudflare) and ericlippert.com (WordPress.com). I did not look into how they are built.

**Patterns**
- **Next.js on Vercel is the most common stack** among the product-side engineers: leerob, joshwcomeau, rauchg and mitchellh. overreacted is also Next.js, hosted on Cloudflare.
- **Posts live in git as Markdown or MDX** almost everywhere. The exceptions are Simon (a Django app with a database) and Karpathy (the Bear Blog hosted service). The classic static generators (Hugo, Jekyll, a custom Go one) belong to the older systems and writing-focused sites: jvns, danluu, brandur and gafferongames.
- **Agent-friendliness is rare and concentrated in the AI-tooling crowd.** Only overreacted and swyx.io serve a real `/llms.txt`. Only steipete.me answers `Accept: text/markdown`, via an Astro site that returns `.md` and sets `Vary: Accept`. Only overreacted and steipete.me serve a per-post `.md` URL. Simon Willison, despite being the loudest voice on LLMs, has none of these; his path is Atom feeds and Datasette. The other nine sites have no markdown route at all.
- **Beware soft 404s.** karpathy.ai returns 200 on `/llms.txt` but serves the HTML homepage. paulgraham.com returns 200 on any `.md` path (html). Always check the content-type.
- **RSS or Atom is near-universal** (every site except karpathy.ai and the leerob and rauchg paths I tried), and the filenames vary (`rss.xml`, `feed.xml`, `atom.xml`, `/feed/`). Feeds are the de facto machine interface.
- **Hosting splits three ways:** Vercel, Cloudflare (in front of origins like Heroku and GitHub Pages) and plain static hosts (Netlify, S3 + CloudFront, Apache, nginx).
- **Interactive or 3D content:** I did not measure it, so this is inferred from what the authors are known for. Josh Comeau and Dan Abramov (React demos) are the main React-widget sites, and iquilezles.org is the main WebGL-demo site. Karpathy, danluu and Paul Graham are deliberately plain.
- **Game devs on this list** run Hugo, hand-built static HTML or self-hosted nginx, not React stacks. I did not find a known indie devlog on Next.js. (inf: this comes from a small sample.)

Result for Village: the stack with the most evidence behind it is Markdown or MDX in git, a static or Next/Astro build, and a deploy host. The cheap agent-friendly extras are `/llms.txt` and per-post `.md`, and steipete.me is the working example of `Accept: text/markdown`.

turns.text:
A fully custom site fits what you described: a 3D landing world, mini-games built with the engine, and engine demos inside posts. Hosting and agent access are the easy parts. The real work is one piece of engine code, explained under "The engine piece".

## What other engineers' sites run on
A Sonnet subagent checked 15 sites live today: headers, page source and the paths agents ask for.
- **Posts are almost always Markdown files in a git repo.** Simon Willison is the exception (a Django app with a database), and so is Karpathy (the hosted Bear Blog service).
- **The most common stack is Next.js hosted on Vercel:** Lee Robinson, Josh Comeau, Guillermo Rauch and Mitchell Hashimoto. Dan Abramov uses Next.js on Cloudflare. Julia Evans, Dan Luu and Brandur run plain static generators. Peter Steinberger's site runs on Astro.
- **Almost nobody serves agents well.** Only Dan Abramov and swyx serve a real `/llms.txt`. Only Peter Steinberger's site returns Markdown when an agent asks for it (the `Accept: text/markdown` header, which Claude Code sends). Karpathy's `/llms.txt` returns the HTML home page.
- **Interactive sites are a small group.** Josh Comeau and Dan Abramov are known for interactive React demos, and Iñigo Quílez for live WebGL. The subagent inferred this from what they're known for and didn't measure it. Game developers mostly keep plain sites.

Your idea is uncommon, and that's an advantage. Hardly anyone pairs a playable world with a properly agent-readable site.

## Reaching agents without the heavy pages
Every page is plain text underneath, and the 3D world is a layer on top.
- Each post is also served as Markdown at `/blog/<post>.md`.
- If an agent asks for Markdown on any URL, it gets the Markdown instead of the 3D page.
- `/llms.txt` is a short map of the site for agents, with RSS and a sitemap alongside.
- The engine's code never loads for agents, for search crawlers, or when a visitor asks for less motion. They all get the fast plain page.

Measured data says most agents don't request `llms.txt` yet: one study found 97% of these files got no requests. It costs almost nothing to add, though. Content negotiation is the part that pays off right away, because coding agents already ask for Markdown.

## Hosting
I'm not suggesting GitHub Pages. It can't return Markdown based on who's asking, and it gives you no server for the fun parts later.

My recommendation is a domain on Cloudflare (sold at cost) and the site on Cloudflare Pages:
- It's free and spreads the site across many locations. A 3D landing page that does well on Hacker News means many visitors downloading the engine at once. One VPS in one data centre would feel that, and a CDN wouldn't.
- A tiny function handles the Markdown answers. Cloudflare's own automatic version of this feature needs a paid plan, so we do it ourselves for free.
- **Your [redacted] VPS stays useful later** for anything that needs a live server: multiplayer mini-games, a guestbook, or high scores.

The alternative is to run everything on the VPS. That gives you full control, but you'd maintain the server and its security certificates yourself, and all traffic would come from one location.

## The engine piece
The landing world, the mini-games and the in-post demos all need the same thing: **a version of the engine that runs from a single file with no server behind it.** It would load a scene and run physics and rendering, without making things or talking to the model. Today the engine's page depends on its local server: `ask.ts`, `link.ts`, `making.ts` and `bay.ts` all call it. How much work that standalone version takes is unknown until I try it, so I'd time-box an experiment. I'd measure how large the download is and how fast it starts on your iPhone, because the landing page has to feel instant.

It also means the engine's code (bundled, not readable source) becomes public. That's in line with your plan to open-source Village, but it's your decision.

## Order of work
1. **The site:** home page, blog, posts as Markdown folders, code highlighting, the `<Claude>` quote block and all the agent features above. I'd build it on Astro, which keeps pages free of JavaScript unless a page needs it. A local preview should take about a day.
2. **The experiment:** the standalone engine playing one saved scene in a page.
3. **Embeds:** `<Scene>` and `<Compare before after>` tags for posts.
4. **The landing world:** a small place you walk through to reach the blog, with easter eggs and physics gags. There's always a plain link to the blog for anyone who just wants to read.

On writing: since you have no preference, start by telling me "new post about X". I'll create the empty post folder, and you write in whatever editor opens it. Publishing is one command.

**Your call:**
- **Go ahead with Cloudflare Pages (recommended)?** I'll start step 1 locally in a new repo, `[redacted]`. Nothing goes public until you've bought a domain and seen a preview.
- **Or would you rather use the [redacted] VPS from the start?**

Sources:
- [llms.txt adoption: 97% of files get no requests (ppc.land)](https://ppc.land/llms-txt-adoption-rises-8-8x-but-97-of-files-get-zero-ai-requests/)
- [Rankability llms.txt adoption tracker](https://www.rankability.com/data/llms-txt-adoption/)
- [Cloudflare: Markdown for Agents](https://developers.cloudflare.com/fundamentals/reference/markdown-for-agents)
- [Search Engine Journal on Cloudflare's Markdown for agents](https://www.searchenginejournal.com/cloudflares-new-markdown-for-ai-bots-what-you-need-to-know/567339/)
- [Answer.AI llms.txt proposal](https://answer.ai/posts/2024-09-03-llmstxt)
- [Josh Comeau: How I Built My Blog](https://www.joshwcomeau.com/blog/how-i-built-my-blog-v2/)

turns.text:
Understood: nothing becomes open source until you say so. I've saved that as a standing rule.

Nothing has been published so far:
- **Village:** the GitHub repo is private. The engine experiment's draft PR goes there, so it stays private.
- **Site:** the new repo at `[redacted]` exists only on your Mac. The builder was told not to create a remote or deploy.
- **Licence:** neither repo has one, and I won't add one.

One related decision for later: putting the site live sends visitors the engine's compiled code, though not its source. I'll ask you before the first public deploy.
